title: Deterministic Polar Subcode Design via Exact Low-Weight Spectrum Characterization
authors: Junhua You, Shaohua Wu, Aolin Liu, Yajing Deng, Qinyu Zhang
abstract:
arXiv:2611.32145v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: We develop a deterministic framework for improving polar-subcode minimum distance through information-set selection and dynamic frozen expression design. Expression design faces two difficulties. Changing an expression can introduce new low-weight codewords, and excluding different codewords can impose conflicting requirements on the same coefficients. To address both difficulties, we first fix the information set and release the editable frozen constraints to form a common supercode containing every candidate code. Its low-weight codewords give necessary and sufficient conditions for one coefficient assignment to exclude every codeword of the specified weights. To apply these conditions at longer lengths, we use the polar decomposition. At each split, a one in the left codeword gives two complementary output bits whose combined weight is always one. We can therefore eliminate the corresponding variables from the parity checks and count their compatible assignments to obtain the exact low-weight spectrum. With both constituent codes fixed, the same reduced checks also simplify the coefficient search. Assignments that give identical check values across all relevant messages share one representative, from which the entire group can be recovered. We give sufficient conditions for choosing the coefficients sequentially without backtracking. Finally, we use the outcome of expression design on one information set to guide exchanges of information positions for the next, linking the two design steps. In experiments spanning block lengths from 64 to 1024 and several code rates, the proposed design meets the target minimum distances in minutes and achieves competitive frame error rates under successive cancellation list decoding.

title: Encrypted Fixed-Point Multiplication in Quasilinear Complexity
authors: Jung Hee Cheon, Junho Lee
abstract:
arXiv:2611.32157v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Homomorphic encryption enables computation on encrypted data, but its high computational overhead remains a central obstacle. We overcome this obstacle asymptotically for high-precision fixed-point arithmetic. In this paper, we introduce focused encoding, which represents a fixed-point number of $n$-bit precision using a polynomial of degree $O(n/\log n)$ over a polynomially bounded modulus by concentrating precision at one embedding. We then introduce an error-shaping technique for homomorphic operations to preserve the encoding. This yields an encrypted fixed-point multiplication algorithm for the CKKS scheme that runs in online time $O(n \log n)$ at $n$-bit precision for any fixed multiplicative depth, with security parameter $\lambda = O(n/\log^2 n)$.
  Further, we develop bootstrapping for focused encoding to overcome the quadratic cost of conventional bootstrapping. We bootstrap ciphertext coefficients at an enlarged scale and shape the resulting error to preserve focused encoding, at the cost of additional modulus consumption. Then, to reduce the remaining logarithmic overhead, we decompose the ciphertext into components over a smaller subring and bootstrap each separately. This reduces the online cost per multiplication, including bootstrapping, to $O(n \log n + n (\log \lambda)^3 \log \log \lambda)$ for security parameter $\lambda = O(n/\log^3 n)$.

title: Low-Degree Torus Approximations of the AND Function and $\mathsf{ACC}^0$ Circuits
authors: Shuhei Osaki, Ryuhei Mori
abstract:
arXiv:2611.32163v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Torus polynomials, real polynomials evaluated modulo one, were proposed by Bhrushundi, Hosseini, Lovett, and Rao as a route to $\mathsf{ACC}^0$ lower bounds. We prove degree upper bounds for torus polynomials approximating a function on every input. First, for every $\epsilon\in(0,1/4)$, $\mathsf{AND}_n/2$ has an $\epsilon$-approximating torus polynomial of degree $O(\log(n/\epsilon))$, improving the previous $O(\log^2(n/\epsilon))$. This is optimal up to constant factors for inverse-polynomial error, by a lower bound of Krishan and Vishwanathan, and refutes two superlogarithmic-degree conjectures of Krishan and Sarma. Second, for every Boolean function $g$ computed by a depth-$d$, size-$s$ $\mathsf{AC}^0[m]$ circuit, $g/2$ has an $\epsilon$-approximating torus polynomial of degree at most $C_m^d(\log s)^{\max\{1,\mu-1\}d}\log(1/\epsilon)$, where $\mu$ is the number of distinct prime factors of $m$ and $C_m$ depends only on $m$. This improves the bound $(\log s)^{O_m(d^2)}(\log(1/\epsilon))^{O_m(d)}$ of Bhrushundi, Hosseini, Lovett, and Rao, making the exponent of $\log s$ linear in the depth and the dependence on $\log(1/\epsilon)$ linear. Both proofs sample terms of a Fourier expansion and approximate them by low-degree torus polynomials. A torus approximation of degree $D$ can be written as a linear combination of at most $(n+1)^D$ parities, called a periodic Fourier representation, which is known to give a non-adaptive measurement-based quantum computation with linear side-processing using one qubit per parity. Hence every $\mathsf{ACC}^0$ function can be computed with quasipolynomially many qubits and inverse-polynomial error probability on every input. Conversely, we prove that a periodic Fourier representation with $r$ parities and error probability $\epsilon$ gives a torus approximation of degree $O(\log(r/\epsilon))$, so the two notions are equivalent.
